claims.text: The steels' corrosion resistance is governed by a self-healing chromium oxide (Cr2O3) passive film.
The as-formed stainless steel naturally has a chromium oxide passivation layer.
Mechanical polishing or acid etching can remove the passive film.
Oxygen availability permits regeneration of the passive film.
A continuous, adherent Cr2O3 layer mediates corrosion resistance.
Chromium in the steel oxidizes during service to form Cr2O3.
The resulting Cr2O3 film is stable under the proposed service conditions.
The Cr2O3 film limits electrolyte access to the underlying metal.
The Cr2O3 film reduces corrosion-reaction kinetics.
Removing the passive film makes the underlying metal more susceptible to rapid oxidation and dissolution.
Film-removed samples will have a measurably higher corrosion rate than untreated samples with an intact film.
The proposed mechanism applies only when the steel contains sufficient chromium.
The mechanism is expected to hold within the selected ranges of acidity, temperature, and radiation exposure.
Nickel and molybdenum may interact with the proposed corrosion-resistance mechanism.
A lack of significantly higher corrosion after film removal would falsify the claim that the chromium oxide layer is the governing cause.

contradictions.description: The film is described as self-healing and exposure includes oxygen that permits its regeneration, yet the prediction assumes that the film-removed group remains meaningfully film-free and the falsification rule treats no sustained corrosion increase as disproof. Rapid repassivation could instead produce no long-term difference while supporting the self-healing mechanism.
